column1: forward-reverse|G|G1|http|A browser explicitly connects to a proxy that fetches arbitrary sites for it. Which role is this?|Forward proxy|Reverse proxy|Authoritative DNS server|Application database replica|A forward proxy acts for clients. A reverse proxy fronts one or more origin services for incoming clients.|Identify which side the proxy represents.

reverse-host|G|G1|http|A public reverse proxy forwards /api to an internal service. Which address is normally contacted by the browser?|The public proxy endpoint|The private backend's loopback address|Every database replica directly|The backend's Unix socket pathname|The proxy mediates the route; internal topology need not be directly visible or reachable from the browser.|Browser reachability and backend reachability differ.

trusted-forwarded|G|G1|rest|An app trusts any X-Forwarded-For header as the client identity. What configuration detail is missing?|Which proxies are trusted to supply that header|The browser's display resolution|The user's HTML color scheme|The database's maximum row size|Client-supplied forwarding metadata can be forged. Trust should depend on the actual proxy path and handling rules.|A header's name does not authenticate its author.

host-port|G|G1|http|Two virtual hosts share one IP and TCP port. Which request data commonly distinguishes them in HTTP/1.1?|Host header authority|The browser's DNS cache TTL|The client's TCP source port alone|The request body's checksum|Name-based virtual hosting selects a site using request authority. Sharing a socket endpoint does not make the applications identical.|One IP address can serve multiple security contexts.

sni-purpose|G|G1|tls|Why may a TLS front end need SNI before receiving HTTP headers?|To select the appropriate TLS virtual-host configuration|To validate the user's SQL permissions|To discover the client's password|To inspect decrypted request body parameters|SNI is part of the TLS handshake, while HTTP request routing occurs later. Certificate selection can depend on it.|Handshake routing precedes application headers.

proxy-error|G|G1|http|A gateway returns 502 after a backend connection fails. What layer reported the error?|The intermediary acting as gateway|The browser's HTML parser|The database necessarily parsing SQL|The client's Ethernet switch|502 indicates a gateway received an invalid upstream response. Determine which component generated the response before attributing the fault.|A visible error may originate before the application.

cache-vary|G|G1|http|A cache serves a language-specific page. What does Vary: Accept-Language tell a compliant cache?|Include that header when selecting a stored response|Never cache any response from the origin|Authenticate the requester through that header|Compress the response using the language code|Vary describes request dimensions affecting representation selection. It is not an authentication policy.|Cache-key selection and permissions are separate controls.

private-cache|G|G1|http|What does Cache-Control: private principally direct shared caches to do?|Avoid storing the response in a shared cache|Encrypt the response with a client-specific key|Invalidate the user's authenticated session|Suppress all copies in the user's own browser|Private concerns shared caching, not encryption or complete client-side retention. Use no-store where storage must be prohibited.|A privacy-sounding cache directive is not encryption.

no-store|G|G4|http|What does Cache-Control: no-store request?|Do not store the request or response in a cache|Store it only on the origin's disk|Store it only after logout|Replace authorization with conditional requests|No-store controls storage by caches; it cannot revoke copies already made elsewhere or prove data was never seen.|A caching instruction is not a universal deletion mechanism.

etag|G|G4|http|What is an ETag primarily used for?|Identifying a representation version for conditional requests|Authenticating a human user|Signing every response with a CA key|Selecting a wireless cipher|An entity tag supports cache validation and conditions such as If-Match. It is not inherently a cryptographic signature.|An opaque tag may be a validator without being a security credential.

if-match|G|G4|http|An update supplies If-Match with an old ETag and receives 412. What likely happened?|The update's precondition was not satisfied|The caller's session was automatically upgraded|The server returned a permanent redirect|The file was necessarily overwritten anyway|Conditional requests can prevent updates based on stale resource versions. A 412 response reports a failed precondition.|Concurrency controls have semantics distinct from authentication errors.

not-modified|G|G4|http|What does 304 Not Modified normally tell a caching client?|Reuse a stored representation after successful validation|The resource was deleted permanently|The request body was accepted for processing|The user's password has changed|304 applies to conditional retrieval and omits representation content. It is not a normal replacement for a 200 body.|Interpret status codes in the method and request context.

head-length|G|G4|http|A HEAD response has Content-Length: 5000 but no response body. Is that necessarily contradictory?|No; metadata can describe the corresponding GET content|Yes; HEAD must return exactly 5000 content bytes|Yes; Content-Length is forbidden in every HEAD response|No; HEAD necessarily downloads a hidden body|HEAD can report representation metadata while omitting content. The length need not be the bytes sent in that response.|Metadata about a representation can differ from bytes transferred now.

content-type-encoding|G|G4|http|Which header describes the media type rather than a compression coding?|Content-Type|Content-Encoding|Transfer-Encoding|Accept-Encoding|Content-Type identifies the representation's media type. Coding and transfer framing are different layers.|Do not equate JSON/HTML types with gzip/chunked handling.

accept-v-content|G|G4|http|A request sends Content-Type: application/json and Accept: text/html. What is the distinction?|JSON describes the request content; HTML describes an acceptable response|Both fields describe the uploaded request body|Both fields force the server to store HTML|The request must contain encrypted HTML|Content-Type labels the sent representation. Accept expresses response preferences; server behavior still needs checking.|Sending format and receiving preference are different directions.

body-method|G|G4|http|Why is moving a password from a URL query into a POST body not sufficient transport protection?|The body still needs a protected connection and safe logging|POST automatically encrypts every field|HTTP proxies cannot observe POST bodies|POST prohibits server-side request logging|Request placement affects exposure surfaces, but TLS and logging controls remain necessary.|A method name is not an encryption mechanism.

put-post|G|G4|http|Which HTTP method conventionally requests replacement of a target resource's state?|PUT|TRACE|HEAD|OPTIONS|PUT has defined resource-update semantics. Actual authorization and implementation determine whether the operation is permitted.|Method semantics do not guarantee permission or implementation.

patch|G|G4|http|What is PATCH conventionally used for?|Applying a partial modification to a resource|Returning metadata without content|Starting a TLS handshake|Listing all names in a DNS zone|PATCH describes partial changes rather than PUT's replacement intent. Applications must validate allowed fields and authority.|Partial update still requires field-level controls.

connect|G|G4|http|What is HTTP CONNECT commonly used for by a forward proxy?|Establishing a tunnel to a specified endpoint|Returning a complete database backup|Deleting every cache entry|Selecting the document's stylesheet|CONNECT creates a tunnel when permitted. Destination restrictions matter because proxy reachability can differ from client reachability.|A tunneling feature changes which endpoints may be reachable.

continue|G|G4|http|A client receives 100 Continue. What does this indicate?|An interim response permitting continuation of the request|Final success of the application operation|A requirement to retry on another hostname|A permanent cache-validity decision|100 is provisional, often concerning sending request content. A later final response determines the outcome.|An interim response is not transaction success.

accepted|G|G4|http|An API returns 202 Accepted for a queued job. What remains unproven?|Successful completion of the job|Acceptance of the request for processing|That processing may occur asynchronously|That a final result needs separate checking|202 does not promise eventual success. A job-status mechanism can provide the final outcome.|Request admission and completed work are different milestones.

conflict|G|G4|http|A version-controlled API update returns 409 Conflict. Which interpretation fits?|The requested change conflicts with current resource state|The caller necessarily supplied a wrong password|The DNS zone necessarily has duplicate records|The server is issuing an authentication challenge|409 concerns state conflict. Details in the response and application workflow establish the exact conflict.|Status labels do not supply all application context.

rate-limit|G|G4|http|An endpoint returns 429 with Retry-After. What behavior is it expressing?|A request-rate limit and suggested retry timing|A permanent deletion of the account|An instruction to disable TLS validation|A guarantee that earlier requests failed|429 signals too many requests; Retry-After can guide retry timing. Assess actual enforcement scope rather than its mere presence.|Rate-limit scope matters: account, IP, token, and action may differ.

webdav|G|G4|http|PROPFIND is associated with which HTTP extension family?|WebDAV|SIP|DHCP|SSH|WebDAV extends HTTP with resource/property operations. A custom method name is not automatically invalid HTTP.|HTTP is extensible beyond the most familiar verbs.

soap-transport|G|G4|xml|Why can a SOAP endpoint require examination beyond its HTTP status codes?|Its XML body defines operations and fault information|SOAP replaces every network transport with UDP|SOAP messages cannot carry user-controlled values|SOAP guarantees authorization for every operation|SOAP is XML-based messaging often carried by HTTP. Operation and fault semantics live in the message as well as the transport.|Transport status and message-level outcome can differ.

soap-fault|G|G4|err|A SOAP response contains a Fault describing a server exception. What should be inspected?|The disclosed fault detail and its application meaning|Only the response's CSS classes|Only the browser's screen size|Only the Ethernet broadcast address|Faults can reveal internal details or describe operation failure. Inspect content without assuming every fault is injection evidence.|Protocol-defined errors can still disclose implementation information.

xml-well-formed|G|G5|xml|What makes XML well-formed at a basic structural level?|Properly nested elements with matching delimiters|Every element name has a public DNS record|Every document is signed with an X.509 key|Every value is encrypted using the same cipher|Well-formedness is a syntax property. Schema validity, trust, and safe parsing impose other requirements.|Syntactic correctness does not mean safe or authorized content.

xml-schema|G|G5|xml|A document is well-formed XML but violates an expected schema. What distinction applies?|Well-formedness and schema validity are different checks|Well-formed XML is necessarily schema-valid|Schema validation decrypts external entities|A schema prevents all authorization defects|A schema can constrain document structure and types. It does not authenticate the requester or safely configure every parser feature.|A structural validator is not a universal security control.

xml-entity|G|G5|xxe|What is an external entity reference capable of directing a permissive XML parser to do?|Resolve content from an external resource|Sign the document with the recipient's key|Enforce row-level database permissions|Upgrade every HTTP connection to TLS|External resolution may involve files or network locations depending on configuration. Safe parser settings constrain the feature.|An XML data format can trigger additional resource access.

html-comment|G|G5|crest|Why can an HTML developer comment be visible even when absent from the rendered page?|The browser receives it in the document source|The comment is necessarily sent by DNS|The comment is automatically encrypted in the DOM|The comment exists only on the server's private disk|Rendered presentation is not the whole received artifact. Source review can reveal paths, clues, or secrets in comments.|Not displayed is not the same as not delivered.

hidden-input|G|G5|authz|What does type=hidden change about a form field?|Its presentation in the ordinary form UI|The server's trust in its submitted value|Its encryption independently of TLS|The user's ability to send a custom request|Hidden fields remain client-controlled. Validate or derive authoritative values on the server.|Visibility is not a trust boundary.

js-runtime|G|G6|crest|Where does JavaScript included in a normal web page primarily execute?|In the receiving browser's execution context|As the database administrator by default|In the router's kernel process|As a privileged OS user on every visitor's machine|Browser code is constrained by origin and browser controls. Server-side JavaScript runtimes are a different deployment context.|The language name does not identify every execution environment.

php-server|G|G6|php|A PHP page prints generated HTML. Which part is normally delivered to the browser?|The output, rather than the original executed PHP source|The entire PHP runtime's internal memory|Every server-side include's private credentials|The database's original password file|Server-side execution produces a response. Misconfiguration or exposed source/backups can change what leaks, so confirm behavior.|Server-side source should not be assumed client-visible.

jsp-servlet|G|G6|crest|How does JSP commonly relate to servlet execution?|A JSP is translated into server-side servlet code|A JSP necessarily runs as browser JavaScript|A servlet is a DNS query type|A JSP disables the Java runtime's access checks|JSP belongs to server-side Java web processing. Client output is a separate representation.|Distinguish server templates from browser scripting.

cgi-interface|G|G8|apache|What is CGI primarily an interface between?|A web server and an external request-handling program|A browser and its graphics card only|A DNS resolver and a mail exchanger|A database and an Ethernet switch|CGI passes request context to a program and obtains its response. The program's input handling and execution rights matter.|An interface exposes a boundary; it does not secure it automatically.

module-worker|G|G8|apache|Why can a native web-server module's memory bug have serious impact?|Its code executes within the server's process context|It necessarily runs only as browser text|It cannot access request data|It has no relationship to server privilege|A module can process untrusted requests within the server. Process identity and isolation determine consequences.|Extension code can inherit a powerful execution environment.

framework-default|G|G7|crest|A framework enables debugging in production. What extra exposure may appear?|Detailed errors or debugging interfaces|Automatic secrecy of all stack traces|Mandatory per-user database isolation|Removal of every HTTP route|Debugging features improve developer visibility but can expose internals. Confirm the enabled feature and reachable behavior.|A development convenience can alter the production attack surface.

ajax-json|G|G7|crest|Does the term AJAX require every modern request to use XML?|No; asynchronous browser requests often use JSON or other formats|Yes; JSON cannot be used by browser requests|Yes; every asynchronous request is a SOAP envelope|No; asynchronous requests can never use HTTP|The historical acronym includes XML, but implementations use multiple representations and browser APIs.|An acronym's history is not a mandatory data format.

ajax-auth|G|G7|authz|An AJAX endpoint is callable without the page that normally invokes it. Which boundary matters?|The endpoint's own authentication and authorization|The page's menu visibility alone|The fact that the caller lacks the stylesheet|The original browser's viewport width|Endpoints must enforce controls independently of the front-end workflow. Custom clients can issue the same HTTP requests.|A page is not the only caller of its API.

client-decompile|G|G9|crest|What can reviewing a distributed .NET thick-client assembly reveal?|Embedded endpoints, logic, and possibly secrets|Only a rendered image of the login screen|Every backend's current memory contents|Every user's authenticated session automatically|Distributed client code is available to recipients for analysis. A recovered secret's validity and authority still need testing.|Client distribution undermines secrecy of embedded constants.

client-secret|G|G9|crest|Why is a credential compiled into a public client application difficult to keep secret?|Recipients control the distributed artifact and execution|Compilation adds strong per-user encryption automatically|The public TLS certificate hides every local constant|The server can prevent all offline inspection of a copied file|Code, configuration, and runtime inspection can recover embedded values. The server should not depend on universal secrecy of shipped credentials.|Obfuscation can raise effort without establishing a trust boundary.

applet-legacy|G|G9|crest|Why should Java applet or ActiveX assessment questions carry a legacy context?|Browser support and execution models have changed substantially|Every current browser executes both by default|The technologies are DNS record types|Both always run only on the database server|Historical syllabus items explain older client attack surfaces. Verify the actual environment rather than assuming current support.|Legacy client components need deployment-specific applicability.

logical-physical|G|G3|crest|Three logical application tiers run on one host. What separation has not necessarily been achieved?|Physical host separation|Separation of software responsibilities|Different logical service roles|A distinct presentation responsibility|Logical layering does not imply independent machines or failure domains. Isolation mechanisms still determine practical boundaries.|Three tiers need not mean three computers.

dmz-db|G|G3|crest|A DMZ web server can connect to an internal database. What must firewall review consider?|The allowed backend path and credential authority|Only the public website's color scheme|Only incoming ICMP echo requests|Only whether the web page uses semantic HTML|An allowed application-to-data flow can become a pivot path after compromise. Narrow network rules and least privilege limit consequences.|A necessary business connection can be an attack-path edge.

shared-account|G|G3|sqlroles|All app servers share one DB login with broad write rights. What grows if one server is compromised?|The reachable data/action scope of that shared credential|The entropy of each user's browser token|The TLS key size on unrelated services|The strength of every table's primary key|Shared powerful credentials enlarge the blast radius. Separate identities and narrower permissions improve containment and attribution.|A shared dependency can couple otherwise separate hosts.

connection-pool|G|G3|crest|What does a database connection pool primarily manage?|Reusable connections between application and database|Every browser user's permanent password hash|Only DNS authoritative zone copies|Only encrypted wireless frame keys|Pooling improves connection reuse. It does not automatically bind each query to a correct end-user authorization decision.|Efficiency mechanisms do not establish access-control policy.

json-parse|G|G5|rest|Why use a data parser rather than eval to read JSON-like input?|Parsing avoids treating input as executable code|Parsing makes all application permissions correct|Parsing encrypts the input's original bytes|Parsing automatically validates every business constraint|A dedicated parser separates representation from execution. Type, business, and authorization checks still follow.|Safe parsing is one boundary, not all boundaries.

content-disposition|G|G4|http|What does Content-Disposition: attachment conventionally influence?|How the client presents a response for download|Whether the requester is authorized to receive it|The server's database encryption key|The number of TLS handshake messages|It suggests download handling and a filename. It is not an access-control decision or a substitute for correct media handling.|Presentation headers cannot authorize data disclosure.

origin-tuple|G|G1|cors|Which tuple normally defines a web origin?|Scheme, host, and port|Path, query string, and fragment|IP address, MAC address, and TTL|Username, password, and session role|Different ports or schemes can define different origins, even on one host. Origin policy and application authorization remain distinct.|Same hostname is not necessarily same origin.

same-site-origin|G|G1|cookies|Why should 'same site' not be treated as identical to 'same origin'?|The site concept groups domains differently from the origin tuple|Every site is a unique TCP connection|Origin is defined only by a cookie's path|Same-site requests are automatically authorized|Cookie site policy and origin isolation use different definitions. Analyze subdomains, schemes, and ports under the relevant mechanism.|Several browser boundaries coexist.

redirect-relative|G|G4|http|A response contains Location: /login. What kind of reference is it?|A relative reference resolved against request context|A complete DNS zone-transfer instruction|A literal filesystem path on every client|An encrypted username hidden in the header|Location may use relative references. Its meaning is a URI reference, not necessarily a server filesystem location.|URL paths and filesystem paths are different namespaces.

server-absolute-path|G|G2|err|An error reveals C:\inetpub\site\config. What has been disclosed?|A likely server-side path and platform clue|Proof that the path is remotely writable|The administrator's valid password|A complete list of virtual-host permissions|Paths can help correlate environment and test hypotheses. Existence, readability, and writability are separate properties.|A path disclosure is not a file-access primitive.

tls-terminator|G|G3|tlscheat|TLS terminates at a proxy and backend HTTP is plaintext. What should an end-to-end confidentiality review include?|Protection of the proxy-to-backend hop|Only the certificate shown to the browser|Only the client's local cookie cache|Only the domain's MX preference|The external TLS channel protects one segment. Trust and network exposure of the backend segment must be evaluated separately.|One protected hop is not every hop.

servlet-state|G|G7|crest|Why can shared mutable state in a server component affect security?|Concurrent users may influence each other's requests|Every server component has exactly one user|Shared state prevents all race conditions|The HTTP protocol prohibits concurrent handling|Request isolation and synchronization matter when instances serve several clients. Test the actual scope of stored state.|Process/component lifetime can exceed one request's lifetime.
